# Decision records

*Generated by `spec render` from the `decisions.yaml` file of each system element. Don't edit this file by hand.*

These are the decisions made while designing and building the toolkit, each attached to the system elements it affects. Reasoning is paraphrased, not quoted.

- ✅ marks a decision you made.
- 🟡 marks a decision an agent made, which needs your review.
- 🔒 marks a decision you've approved, 🔓 one that changed since you approved it, and ⤷ one delegated under an item you approved.

### DR-1 ✅ 🔒 The CLI is the product, the method is one portable skill, and harness glue is optional
*System elements:* SYS, CLI, AGENT · *Requirements:* SYS-5, SYS-27, CLI-1 · *Recorded:* round 6 (Q21). A Claude Code plugin was first proposed in round 1.
- **Context:** I first proposed packaging the toolkit as a Claude Code plugin. The engineer wants to use the method in other agent setups as well (Antigravity next, still with Claude models), so it shouldn't be tied to one harness.
- **Decision:** the Python CLI holds all the logic. The method ships as one Agent Skill in the open SKILL.md format, which Claude Code, Antigravity and most other harnesses read. A harness can also get thin glue that calls the CLI; the setup command writes that glue into the repository. There is no plugin.
- **Alternatives:** a Claude Code plugin as the product (the first proposal). The CLI and the skill only, with no glue anywhere, which leaves the merge-time check as the only hard gate.
- **Consequences:** Claude Code is the first harness with glue (DR-3, DR-4, DR-6, DR-7). In a harness without glue, those enforcements become instructions, and the merge-time check (CHECK-15) is the backstop.

### DR-2 🟡 🔒 Store the spec as YAML, and take edits as a YAML batch on standard input
*System elements:* MODEL, CLI · *Requirements:* MODEL-1, CLI-1, CLI-7 · *Recorded:* round 4 (decided in round 2; approved in round 5)
- **Context:** the engineer chose the CLI as the agents' way to edit the spec, so that it can add context before an edit lands. The format was left to me.
- **Decision:** spec files are YAML. To make several edits, an agent writes them as one small YAML document and pipes it into a single CLI command, usually as a heredoc. That avoids passing each field as a command-line argument.
- **Alternatives:** JSON edited only through the CLI, which was the engineer's first idea but produces noisy diffs. Markdown with embedded metadata, which is fragile to parse.
- **Consequences:** raw git diffs stay readable, prose never fights shell quoting, and a large update is one call.

### DR-3 🟡 🔒 Refuse direct edits to spec files with a pre-tool hook
*System elements:* AGENT · *Requirements:* AGENT-20 · *Recorded:* round 4 (decided in round 2)
- **Status:** part of the Claude Code adapter (DR-1). Other harnesses get an equivalent where they offer the hooks for it.
- **Context:** agents are trained to edit files directly, which would bypass the CLI's context step.
- **Decision:** a Claude Code PreToolUse hook refuses agents' file edits under the spec directory. Its refusal names the CLI command to use instead.
- **Alternatives:** an instruction in the skill, which is easy to ignore. Linting afterwards, by which time the edit has already happened.
- **Consequences:** the engineer can still edit spec files by hand, because hooks only see agents' tool calls.

### DR-4 🟡 🔒 Run the checker from a stop hook
*System elements:* AGENT, CHECK · *Requirements:* AGENT-12, CHECK-12 · *Recorded:* round 4 (decided in round 1)
- **Status:** part of the Claude Code adapter (DR-1). Other harnesses get an equivalent where they offer the hooks for it.
- **Context:** the main agent often won't have the methodology in context, and it may forget to run the checker.
- **Decision:** a Claude Code Stop hook runs the checker when the agent tries to finish, and blocks with the findings. It blocks at most once per turn, so a mid-task question to the engineer still gets through.
- **Alternatives:** relying on the skill's instructions. A CI-only check, which comes too late.
- **Consequences:** the checker must be fast (CHECK-12).

### DR-5 🟡 🔒 Approval records store a fingerprint and the approved content
*System elements:* MODEL · *Requirements:* MODEL-24, MODEL-25, REVIEW-11 · *Recorded:* round 4 (the fingerprint idea is the engineer's, from round 2; storing the content was MODEL-26)
- **Context:** the engineer proposed recording approvals with a hash or git state, so the toolkit can tell when approved content has changed.
- **Decision:** each approval stores the item's fingerprint and the approved text itself.
- **Alternatives:** a fingerprint alone, which shows *that* something changed but not *what*. A git revision, which fails for approvals given before a commit.
- **Consequences:** the review page can always show what changed since approval. [approvals.md](approvals.md) already follows this format by hand.

### DR-6 🟡 🔓 Record chat approvals from the engineer's own message
*System elements:* AGENT · *Requirements:* AGENT-21, AGENT-33, AGENT-34 · *Recorded:* round 4 (decided in round 3)
- **Status:** part of the Claude Code adapter (DR-1). Other harnesses get an equivalent where they offer the hooks for it. Narrowed in round 11 by DR-41: the hook records only approvals that name items by ID, and anything else is confirmed with the engineer first.
- **Context:** the engineer wants to approve in chat, but only with unambiguous wording.
- **Decision:** a Claude Code UserPromptSubmit hook reads the engineer's message. When the message is an explicit approval, the hook records it against the items as they were last shown. Approvals the hook can't read, such as a choice in the harness's question menu or an explicit "<ID> LGTM", are recorded by the agent, quoting the engineer's words and naming the channel.
- **Alternatives:** letting the agent record approvals, which risks a misreading. Approving only on the review page, which is safe but slower.
- **Consequences:** Q23 settled the phrasing: a message that starts with "approve" and names the items, or says to approve everything except some items. When the exceptions are given by description, every item they could refer to stays unapproved (AGENT-43). In harnesses without such a hook, chat approval falls back to the review page or the terminal.

### DR-7 🟡 🔓 Run reasoning checks in an isolated subagent that can't see the spec
*System elements:* REASON · *Requirements:* REASON-2, REASON-5 · *Recorded:* round 4 (was REASON-6 and REASON-7)
- **Status:** part of the Claude Code adapter (DR-1). The requirement itself is harness-neutral (DR-25): the skill describes the ideal reasoning-check subagent, and each agent sets one up with what its harness offers. This record covers how to do that in Claude Code. Q22 ruled out an API path. Refined in round 11 by DR-42: searches that could reach the spec are refused rather than filtered.
- **Context:** the engineer wants reasoning checks to start with no project context and no conversation, and to read the code but not the spec.
- **Decision:** use a custom, non-fork subagent. Its definition sets `omitClaudeMd`, so CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md don't load. It has no shell tool. It carries its own hook that refuses reads under the spec directory and drops spec hits from search results.
- **Alternatives:** a fork, which inherits the conversation and which the engineer ruled out. An instruction alone. A direct model-API call, which Q22 ruled out (DR-25).
- **Consequences:** if the read-blocking hook proves fiddly, drop it and keep the instruction (the engineer's call).

### DR-8 🟡 🔒 A decomposition tree plus a separate dependency graph
*System elements:* MODEL · *Requirements:* MODEL-3, MODEL-4, MODEL-11 · *Recorded:* round 4 (decided in round 1)
- **Context:** the engineer's first sketch had one "depends on" relation that covered both "is part of" and "uses".
- **Decision:** "part of" is a tree, so each system element has one parent. "Uses" is a separate graph that must have no cycles.
- **Alternatives:** one combined graph, which mixes requirement flow-down with change impact. Several parents per element.
- **Consequences:** requirements flow down the tree, and change impact follows the dependency graph. A shared element, such as a general utility, has one parent: usually the lowest element whose parts all use it, or the system itself. Every element that relies on it lists it as a dependency. Q24 confirmed this and added one rule: verifying a change also covers every element that depends on what it touched (VERIFY-14).

### DR-9 🟡 🔒 Wording rules from INCOSE plus EARS patterns
*System elements:* MODEL · *Requirements:* MODEL-16 · *Recorded:* round 4 (decided in round 1)
- **Context:** the engineer asked for hard, checkable rules for writing requirements.
- **Decision:** use the mechanically checkable subset of INCOSE's Guide to Writing Requirements: one "shall"; no vague terms, escape clauses or open-ended endings; no test or implementation vocabulary. Add the EARS sentence patterns.
- **Alternatives:** a free-form style judged only by a model, which can't be verified. INCOSE's full set of roughly 40 rules, many of which need judgment.
- **Consequences:** the checker can enforce wording. Q25 made every rule an error.
  - Each finding names its rule, says why the rule exists, and suggests a rewrite (CHECK-16).
  - Findings link to the skill's own rules page, which cites INCOSE's rule numbers, because the INCOSE guide isn't freely available.
  - To save tokens, a rule is explained in full only once per run (CHECK-17).
  - The aim is the Rust compiler's style: errors that teach a fresh agent this repo's expectations. Quality that needs judgment is left to the auditors (SYS-21).

### DR-10 ✅ 🔒 Related code is a loose link, not file ownership
*System elements:* MODEL, CHECK · *Requirements:* MODEL-10, CHECK-5, CHECK-8 · *Recorded:* round 4 (decided in round 2)
- **Context:** I first proposed that each file belong to exactly one system element. The engineer worried that this would make refactoring costly and tie the spec to one language's file layout.
- **Decision:** each system element lists related code by path or pattern, and a file may relate to any number of elements. Tests are the firm link.
- **Alternatives:** exactly-one ownership. Deriving the mapping from per-test coverage, which may come later as an upgrade.
- **Consequences:** some code may relate to no system element. CHECK-8 flags such code when it changes.

### DR-11 ✅ 🔒 Adopt systems-engineering vocabulary
*System elements:* SYS · *Requirements:* the whole spec, MODEL-30 · *Recorded:* round 4
- **Context:** the engineer had coined "component" and "item" and wanted the vocabulary to follow best practice.
- **Decision:** "system element" replaces "component". Verification items name one of the four standard methods (test, analysis, demonstration, inspection) and a technique (unit test, integration test, reasoning check). The full vocabulary is in [glossary.md](glossary.md).
- **Alternatives:** keep "component", which is familiar to software engineers but isn't the standard term.
- **Consequences:** agents that know SE terms can apply them directly.

### DR-12 ✅ 🔒 Scenarios of use are context on needs, not an item type
*System elements:* MODEL · *Requirements:* MODEL-29 · *Recorded:* round 4
- **Context:** I proposed a separate item type for the engineer's CUJs. The engineer preferred annotating needs with them, so that future agents know why a need exists.
- **Decision:** each need records its context in paraphrase: the reasoning and the scenarios behind it.
- **Alternatives:** a scenario item type with its own IDs and approvals.
- **Consequences:** this matches SE practice, which keeps operational scenarios in a narrative concept-of-operations document rather than as baselined line items.

### DR-13 ✅ 🔒 No transcript archive; decision records carry the reasoning
*System elements:* MODEL, AGENT · *Requirements:* SYS-19, MODEL-28, AGENT-24, AGENT-35 · *Recorded:* round 4 (decided in round 3)
- **Context:** the engineer first suggested linking conversation transcripts. Claude Code deletes those after 30 days by default, they live on one machine, and they can contain secrets.
- **Decision:** keep no transcript links and no archive. Each decision becomes a dated, paraphrased decision record on the system elements it affects.
- **Alternatives:** archive transcripts outside the repository, or raise the retention period.
- **Consequences:** reasoning has to be captured when the decision is made. This file does that for rounds 1–5.

### DR-14 ✅ 🔒 Expensive verification only when the engineer asks
*System elements:* VERIFY, AGENT · *Requirements:* SYS-12, AGENT-30 · *Recorded:* round 4 (decided in rounds 2 and 3)
- **Context:** reasoning checks and long runs cost tokens and time. The engineer wants to move fast and to decide when these run.
- **Decision:** expensive items run only when the engineer asks: for a full run, a single change, or onboarding (ONBOARD-3). Agents always run every cheap item before reporting a change as done.
- **Alternatives:** running expensive items automatically at merge, which was my first proposal.
- **Consequences:** regressions that only expensive checks would catch wait for the next requested run.

### DR-15 ✅ 🔒 Code-first never stops to ask; only spec-first may
*System elements:* AGENT · *Requirements:* SYS-16, SYS-18, AGENT-18 · *Recorded:* round 4 (decided in round 3)
- **Context:** the engineer wants to hand off a change, come back to it finished, and read the spec. Stopping to ask belongs to planning.
- **Decision:** in code-first mode, agents finish the change and report every contradiction and question at the end. In spec-first mode, an agent may stop on a contradiction the engineer would likely want to decide first.
- **Alternatives:** stopping in either mode whenever the agent judges a contradiction important. That was the engineer's first answer, refined in round 3.
- **Consequences:** a code-first change may be built on a reading the engineer later rejects. The open decisions make that visible immediately.

### DR-16 ✅ 🔒 Defer verifying agent-behavior requirements
*System elements:* AGENT · *Requirements:* the AGENT requirements · *Recorded:* round 4 (decided in round 3)
- **Context:** the AGENT requirements describe judgments, such as when to stop and ask, which unit tests can't check. The engineer wants to start building and iterate.
- **Decision:** verify them by demonstration, meaning the engineer observes them in real use, until an eval harness exists.
- **Alternatives:** build scenario evals now.
- **Consequences:** following current eval guidance, the first eval scenarios should come from real failures seen in use.

### DR-17 🟡 🔒 Independence through review, not separate authors
*System elements:* AGENT · *Requirements:* SYS-11, AGENT-13, AGENT-14, AGENT-31 · *Recorded:* round 4 (decided in round 2)
- **Context:** in the engineer's experience, requirements and their verification should have different authors. In code-first mode, one agent writes the code, the tests and the spec.
- **Decision:** checks come from fresh-context auditors that didn't author the change. One auditor examines only the tests and verification items that the change modified or deleted.
- **Alternatives:** separate authoring agents for requirements and for verification, which was the earlier spec-first design.
- **Consequences:** this removes the incentive to go easy. It doesn't remove blind spots shared by every instance of one model.

### DR-18 ✅ 🔒 Restructure the spec into layers
*System elements:* SYS · *Requirements:* SYS-6 to SYS-27 · *Recorded:* round 4
- **Context:** by round 3 the spec held 142 requirements at the element level, and almost none of them traced to a need. That was too much to read, and it diverged from SE's flow-down.
- **Decision:** needs come first, then system requirements that serve them, then element requirements, each tracing to exactly one system requirement. Design choices moved into this file.
- **Alternatives:** a flat list grouped by system element.
- **Consequences:** the layer to read is now needs, system requirements and constraints. Q20 then removed restatements (DR-22).

### DR-19 🟡 🔒 Named acknowledgments only for edits with impact
*System elements:* CLI · *Requirements:* CLI-6 · *Recorded:* round 4 (decided in round 2)
- **Context:** the engineer wanted the CLI to show context before an edit and ask for confirmation. Models rubber-stamp generic confirmations.
- **Decision:** an edit that touches approved or depended-upon items needs an acknowledgment of each affected item, by name, with a one-line note. Other edits apply at once.
- **Alternatives:** a generic confirmation on every edit, or no confirmation.
- **Consequences:** friction appears only where there's something to weigh, and the notes become reasons the engineer can read.

### DR-20 ✅ 🔒 Importance is judged from history, not stored as a flag
*System elements:* MODEL, AGENT, REASON · *Requirements:* SYS-24, SYS-26, MODEL-14, REASON-4, AGENT-15, AGENT-16, AGENT-40 · *Recorded:* round 5
- **Context:** I proposed a "critical" flag on requirements, which would trigger extra verification. The engineer worried that such a flag inflates over time until it means nothing. The engineer preferred that agents judge importance from each item's recorded history, for deciding both how much to verify and what to ask about first.
- **Decision:** there is no criticality flag. Agents judge importance each time from an item's history: whether the engineer stated it, its decision records, how often it changed, and what depends on it. They state their reasons whenever they act on a judgment (AGENT-40).
- **Alternatives:** a stored critical flag (MODEL-19 and MODEL-20, now removed).
- **Consequences:** judgments can differ between runs. Stated reasons make that visible and correctable.

### DR-21 ✅ 🔒 Onboarding records the current state with maximum agent effort
*System elements:* ONBOARD · *Requirements:* SYS-23, ONBOARD-1 to ONBOARD-7 · *Recorded:* round 5
- **Context:** I had proposed adopting the toolkit gradually, grandfathering existing gaps in a baseline (CHECK-13). The engineer wants the opposite. Bringing a project in should capture everything at once, as carefully as possible, so that the engineer only confirms the needs and approves the rest. Reviewing an existing project line by line would take forever.
- **Decision:** onboarding extracts the full spec and the reasons behind it, runs every check (including expensive ones and auditors), and asks only questions the project can't answer. It records the current state without proposing changes. Rigor goes into later changes instead.
- **Alternatives:** gradual adoption with a shrinking baseline of grandfathered findings.
- **Consequences:** onboarding is expensive in tokens and time, but it happens once per project.

### DR-22 ✅ 🔒 No restatement; system requirements can be allocated directly
*System elements:* SYS, MODEL · *Requirements:* MODEL-33 · *Recorded:* round 5
- **Context:** after layering, several element requirements just repeated their parent. The engineer counts every repeated line as wasted attention (NEED-11).
- **Decision:** remove requirements that only restate their parent. A system requirement can be allocated to a system element without an element-level copy. Round 5 removed eleven restatements.
- **Alternatives:** keep the copies, so that each system element "owns" its requirements.
- **Consequences:** less to read. Allocation is shown on the system requirement itself.

### DR-23 ✅ 🔒 System requirements are verified at the system level
*System elements:* MODEL, VERIFY · *Requirements:* MODEL-32 · *Recorded:* round 5
- **Context:** SE verifies each level at its own level (the V-model). Passing element-level tests doesn't prove the system works end to end.
- **Decision:** each system requirement gets its own verification, such as an end-to-end run or a demonstration, in addition to its children's verification.
- **Alternatives:** treat a system requirement as verified when all its children pass.
- **Consequences:** the VI round will write system-level checks, for example running a code-first change end to end and confirming that it never stopped to ask.

### DR-24 ✅ 🔒 Open decisions come with options and a recommendation
*System elements:* CHANGE · *Requirements:* CHANGE-10, CHANGE-11, CHANGE-12 · *Recorded:* round 5
- **Context:** the engineer wants to settle agent-raised issues quickly, often accepting a whole set at once. When something the engineer wrote, or something with recorded history, is involved, the engineer wants a warning not to skim it.
- **Decision:** every open decision offers options, with one marked as recommended, and a set can be accepted in one statement. Each one also says whether it involves an engineer-stated item or one with decision records behind it. That last part is my extension (CHANGE-11) from flagged items to all open decisions.
- **Alternatives:** free-form questions.
- **Consequences:** most decisions take seconds. The ones that touch your own words stand out.

### DR-25 ✅ 🔒 A harness that can start subagents is required, and the skill states outcomes, not means
*System elements:* SYS, AGENT, REASON · *Requirements:* SYS-28, SYS-29, AGENT-41, AGENT-42, REASON-2 · *Recorded:* round 8 (Q22)
- **Context:** Q22 asked whether reasoning checks need a path that runs outside any agent harness. The engineer decided that a harness is always involved and must be able to start subagents. The skill's job is to say what's needed and how a subagent should ideally be set up. How to do it is up to each agent and its harness. More broadly, agents should use whatever their harness offers, such as question menus, to make the experience good.
- **Decision:** the toolkit assumes an agent harness that can start subagents, and there's no model-API path. The skill's language stays generic enough for Claude Code, Antigravity, Codex and future harnesses. It states outcomes and ideal setups, and leaves the means to the agent.
- **Alternatives:** an API path added later (my recommendation in Q22), or an API path only.
- **Consequences:** reasoning checks can't run in plain CI without an agent. Instructions specific to one harness live only in that harness's adapter (DR-1).

### DR-26 ✅ 🔒 Order questions by how much their answers would change
*System elements:* CHANGE, AGENT · *Requirements:* SYS-26, AGENT-40 · *Recorded:* round 8
- **Context:** a ranked list worked well for the engineer. It sorted the questions by how much each answer would change, said why each ranked where it did, gave a recommended option, and offered a one-line way to accept everything. The engineer wants the skill to do this whenever it asks questions or flags things.
- **Decision:** order questions and flags by how likely each answer is to change the spec or the other answers, most consequential first. Each one carries its reasons and a recommended option, and a set can be accepted in one line.
- **Alternatives:** ordering by system element or by ID.
- **Consequences:** the engineer can stop after the top few. The rest can usually be accepted as a block.

### DR-27 ✅ 🔒 IDs always come with a title, linked where possible
*System elements:* AGENT, REVIEW · *Requirements:* SYS-30, AGENT-44, REVIEW-15 · *Recorded:* round 8
- **Context:** the engineer can't remember what an ID refers to, and bare IDs send them searching files.
- **Decision:** every mention of a spec item gives its title alongside its ID, and links to it where the medium allows. The review page shows an item's text when you hover over or click its ID.
- **Alternatives:** bare IDs, or titles only. Titles alone would lose the stable reference that traceability needs.
- **Consequences:** messages run slightly longer, and nothing needs to be looked up.

### DR-28 🟡 🔒 The spec lives in YAML files per system element, and the Markdown views are generated
*System elements:* MODEL, REVIEW · *Requirements:* MODEL-1, MODEL-25, MODEL-28, REVIEW-14 · *Recorded:* round 9 (slice 1)
- **Context:** DR-2 chose YAML, and slice 1 had to choose the files. The engineer reads Markdown, and diffs should stay small and local to what changed.
- **Decision:** Each system element is a directory under spec/elements/. It holds element.yaml, plus requirements.yaml, verification.yaml and decisions.yaml as needed.
  - Needs live with the system element.
  - A decision record sits with the first element it names.
  - Approvals, retired IDs, questions and project settings are single files at the top of spec/.
  - requirements.md and decisions.md are generated by `spec render`, and the checker reports them when they're stale.
- **Alternatives:** One big YAML file, which becomes a merge-conflict hotspot. One file per item, which means hundreds of tiny files. Hand-written Markdown as the source, which can't be parsed reliably and drifts.
- **Consequences:** A change to one element touches one directory, and readers keep the same Markdown view. Hand edits to a view are overwritten, and the checker flags them first.

### DR-29 🟡 🔒 Fingerprints cover an item's meaning, and migration carried approvals over
*System elements:* MODEL · *Requirements:* MODEL-24, MODEL-25, MODEL-31 · *Recorded:* round 9 (slice 1)
- **Context:** Approvals were fingerprints of Markdown text. Moving to YAML would have broken every one of them, even though no meaning changed.
- **Decision:** A fingerprint is a hash of an item's meaning fields, which vary by kind:
  - requirement: its text;
  - need: its text and context;
  - decision record: its title, status, context, decision, alternatives and consequences;
  - verification item: its description, method, technique and the requirements it verifies;
  - system element: its title, purpose, parent and dependencies.
  Before migrating, every old fingerprint was checked against the Markdown, and all 69 matched. The approvals were then re-fingerprinted, with each old value kept as `migrated_from`.
- **Alternatives:** Asking the engineer to re-approve 69 unchanged items. Fingerprinting the raw YAML, which would let a formatting change un-approve an item.
- **Consequences:** Re-formatting or re-linking an item never un-approves it, and rewording it always does. One old fingerprint, NEED-12's, had also covered the heading of the next section, because of a parsing bug in my interim scripts. Its new fingerprint covers just the need and its context.

### DR-30 🟡 🔒 Wording rules were calibrated against this spec before they shipped
*System elements:* CHECK, MODEL · *Requirements:* MODEL-16, CHECK-16 · *Recorded:* round 9 (slice 1)
- **Context:** The engineer chose strict wording rules (errors, not warnings), so a noisy rule would block agents on false alarms and teach them to fight the checker. The checker's first run on this spec reported 29 errors, and 18 of them were false.
- **Decision:** - EARS is read loosely: condition clauses at the front are optional (When, While, If, Where, In, During, At and similar), and the subject may contain commas.
  - The check for conditions placed after "shall" was dropped. Only 1 of its 10 hits was real, because phrases like "decisions made while building" aren't conditions. Auditors judge condition placement instead.
  - Three exemptions cover the remaining false hits: "how many", capitalized words inside a proper name, and "both … and".
  - The other 11 findings were real, and those requirements were reworded.
- **Alternatives:** Keeping every rule as first written and rewording around the false hits, which bends good requirements to fit bad rules. Turning the noisy rules into warnings, which the engineer had ruled out.
- **Consequences:** Every remaining rule fires only on real problems in this spec. Each exemption has a regression test, so a later change to the rules can't silently bring the noise back.

### DR-31 🟡 🔓 Missing verification, missing approvals and unserved needs are to-dos, not errors
*System elements:* CHECK · *Requirements:* CHECK-10, CHECK-14, CHECK-15, MODEL-18, SYS-9 · *Recorded:* round 9 (slice 1)
- **Context:** 169 requirements have no verification item yet, and most items aren't approved. If those were errors, the checker would fail on every run, and agents would learn to ignore it.
- **Decision:** They're reported as to-dos, summarized in one line and listed by `spec check --todo`. Only errors fail the check. The done gate (CHECK-11) will make missing verification an error for the requirements a change touches. A need that no requirement serves yet is a to-do too, so needs can be recorded before the requirements that serve them, as spec-first planning does (round 12). The merge check (`spec check --merge`, CHECK-15) never fails because of approvals: whether a branch lands is the engineer's call (round 12, D1).
- **Alternatives:** Failing on every missing item from day one.
- **Consequences:** The checker stays green while to-dos remain, so the summary line is what keeps them visible.

### DR-32 🟡 🔓 A Nix flake for development, and standard packaging for everyone else
*System elements:* SYS · *Requirements:* SYS-3 · *Recorded:* round 9 (slice 1)
- **Context:** The engineer's machine runs NixOS, where generic Linux binaries such as uv's installer don't run. The engineer's other project already uses a flake.
- **Decision:** flake.nix provides Python with PyYAML and pytest for working on the toolkit, and `bin/spec` runs the CLI from the checkout. pyproject.toml keeps the toolkit installable with pip everywhere else. Nothing outside this repository's own development setup depends on Nix (SYS-32).
- **Alternatives:** A pip virtual environment, which works here but isn't the engineer's convention.
- **Consequences:** Agents run `spec` from the PATH, as in any other repository. On the engineer's machine it's installed with `pipx install --editable` from this checkout, so changes apply at once (DR-52).

### DR-33 🟡 🔒 Change records are YAML, one change is open at a time, and every edit needs one
*System elements:* CHANGE · *Requirements:* CHANGE-3, CHANGE-4, CHANGE-5, CHANGE-8, CHANGE-9 · *Recorded:* round 10 (slice 2)
- **Context:** Change records were hand-written Markdown, so nothing checked them and reasons were tracked by hand.
- **Decision:** A change record is spec/changes/<date>-round-<N>[-<slug>].yaml, with a generated Markdown view beside it.
  - `spec change start` opens one, with a summary of the request, the mode (code-first unless named) and the target implementation (the primary one unless named).
  - At most one change is open at a time, and `spec edit` refuses to run without one.
  - Rounds 2 to 9 stay as hand-written Markdown, and `spec show` still finds mentions in them.
- **Alternatives:** Logging edits in git commit messages, which fragments the reasons across commits and the engineer owns git anyway. Several open changes, which forces every edit to name its change.
- **Consequences:** Every edit's reason lands in one place the engineer reads. Starting a change is one extra command per change.

### DR-34 🟡 🔒 An edit runs on a scratch copy first, and only the errors it introduces block it
*System elements:* CLI, CHECK · *Requirements:* CLI-5, CLI-7, SYS-25 · *Recorded:* round 10 (slice 2)
- **Context:** The engineer wanted the CLI to intercept edits and surface problems before they land. Pre-existing errors elsewhere in the spec shouldn't block an unrelated edit.
- **Decision:** `spec edit` copies the spec, applies the whole batch there, and runs the checker on the result. An error that wasn't there before rejects the batch, with the usual teaching messages, and nothing is written. Otherwise the batch is applied for real, logged and re-rendered. `--dry-run` stops after the checks.
- **Alternatives:** Validating each operation on its own, which misses problems that only appear once the whole batch is applied. Rejecting any batch while any error exists, which blocks repairs.
- **Consequences:** A batch is all or nothing. Copying the spec costs a fraction of a second at this size.

### DR-35 🟡 🔒 Acknowledgments are needed only when an item's meaning changes
*System elements:* CLI · *Requirements:* CLI-6 · *Recorded:* round 10 (slice 2)
- **Context:** DR-19 asked for named acknowledgments when an edit touches approved or depended-on items. Building it showed that a rationale-only edit, or a re-pointed test link, would have demanded acknowledgments for nothing.
- **Decision:** An edit needs an acknowledgment only when it changes an item's meaning, which its fingerprint detects, or removes the item. The items that need one are:
  - the item itself, if approved;
  - the requirements that refine it;
  - requirements serving it, if it's a need;
  - the verification items that verify it;
  - the decision records about it;
  - for a system element, the elements that depend on it or are part of it.
  The CLI prints a ready-to-fill `acks:` block, and exits with code 2.
- **Alternatives:** Acknowledging every touched item, which is pure friction for wording and link edits. No acknowledgments at all, which the engineer ruled out.
- **Consequences:** The acknowledgment notes land in the change record, as reasons the engineer can read.

### DR-36 🟡 🔒 Removing an item retires its ID, and new IDs are allocated automatically
*System elements:* CLI, MODEL · *Requirements:* MODEL-15, CLI-7 · *Recorded:* round 10 (slice 2)
- **Context:** IDs must never be reused (MODEL-15). Agents picking numbers by hand would collide or reuse.
- **Decision:** A removal moves the ID into retired.yaml with its reason, and drops the item's approval. A new item gets the next number after the highest live or retired ID with its prefix. An explicit `id` is still accepted, unless it's taken or retired.
- **Alternatives:** Leaving tombstones in place in the element files, which clutters the files every agent reads.
- **Consequences:** Agents never choose numbers, and a retired ID can't come back by accident.

### DR-37 🟡 🔒 The change log records every changed field, not just meaning
*System elements:* CHANGE · *Requirements:* CHANGE-5, AGENT-14, REVIEW-9 · *Recorded:* round 10 (slice 2)
- **Context:** The first version logged only meaning fields. A test-link change showed up as an empty diff, and re-pointed tests are exactly where test weakening hides.
- **Decision:** Each log entry records the fields that changed, before and after, test links included. Meaning-only comparison is kept for deciding when acknowledgments are needed.
- **Alternatives:** Logging meaning only, which hides test changes from auditors.
- **Consequences:** One entry from round 10 (MODEL-V7's new test links) was logged before this fix, so it carries a reason but no field diff.

### DR-38 🟡 ⤷SYS-27 The skill ships inside the package, and setup installs it with the launcher's name filled in
*System elements:* AGENT, CLI · *Requirements:* AGENT-42, SYS-27, CLI-9 · *Recorded:* round 11 (slice 3)
- **Status:** superseded in round 17 by DR-53 on where the skill is installed. Its rules for the skill's content still hold.
- **Context:** The method is one portable skill (DR-1). It has to reach each repository, and the commands it gives have to work there however the machine installs Python.
- **Decision:** The skill lives in the Python package, so installing the toolkit installs it. It is SKILL.md plus four reference pages: writing requirements, auditing, onboarding, and the rules page the checker links to.
  - `spec init` writes one copy, in .agents/skills/syseng, the cross-tool location Hermes and Antigravity read. For Claude Code, which reads only .claude/skills, .claude/skills/syseng is a link to that copy. Hermes loads a repository's skills only after `hermes skills trust`.
  - The copy is the skill exactly as written: it has no placeholders and names no harness, tool or package manager.
  - What each harness's hooks do goes in the instruction-file section, which every harness reads.
- **Alternatives:** A skill that tells agents to run `spec` from the PATH, which breaks whenever the toolkit lives in a virtual environment the agent's shell hasn't activated. Keeping the skill outside the package, which pip wouldn't install.
- **Consequences:** The installed copy is committed with the repository, so it can fall behind the toolkit; `spec init --check` reports the difference and `spec init` refreshes it. A checkout on a system without symlinks would see the link as a plain file, and Claude Code would miss the skill there. The rules page moved from docs/ into the skill.

### DR-39 🟡 ⤷SYS-5 Two launchers, one committed with the repository and one per machine
*System elements:* CLI · *Requirements:* SYS-5, SYS-32, CLI-9 · *Recorded:* round 11 (slice 3)
- **Status:** superseded in round 15 by DR-52, which runs the toolkit as `spec` from the PATH.
- **Context:** Agents need one command that runs the toolkit in every checkout, including worktrees and teammates' clones, while each machine installs Python its own way. The engineer asked that Nix not be assumed (SYS-32).
- **Decision:** `.syseng/spec` is a short shell script, committed with the repository. It runs this machine's launcher, ${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-~/.config}/syseng/launcher.
  - `spec init` writes the machine's launcher to run the Python that ran `spec init`, adding the toolkit's source directory when the toolkit isn't installed as a package.
  - `--launcher CMD` replaces it, for setups such as a Nix shell. An existing launcher that works is otherwise kept.
  - Without a machine launcher, `.syseng/spec` says the toolkit isn't set up and exits with code 127.
- **Alternatives:** One launcher per repository, ignored by git, which new worktrees and fresh clones don't have. Running `spec` from the PATH, which depends on which environment is active.
- **Consequences:** `spec init` writes one file outside the repository. A machine with two toolkit installs uses whichever one `spec init --launcher` named last.

### DR-40 🟡 ⤷SYS-27 Claude Code hooks are one standard-library script, committed with the repository
*System elements:* AGENT · *Requirements:* AGENT-20, AGENT-12, SYS-27 · *Recorded:* round 11 (slice 3)
- **Context:** The spec guard (DR-3), the done gate (DR-4) and chat approvals (DR-6) need hooks. The guard runs before every edit and shell command, so it must be fast, and it should work on a clone where the toolkit isn't installed yet.
- **Decision:** `.syseng/hook` is one Python script that uses only the standard library. `spec init` copies it from the package and registers it in .claude/settings.json for three events: before each tool call, when the agent stops, and when the engineer sends a message.
  - It refuses a tool call by exiting with code 2, giving the reason on standard error.
  - The guard refuses edits to the files the toolkit manages: elements, change records, approvals, retired IDs and generated views. Its refusal names the command to use. toolkit.yaml and hand-written pages such as the glossary stay editable.
  - For shell commands, it refuses plain writes into those files: redirections, tee, rm, mv, cp, and in-place sed or perl.
  - When the agent stops with errors in the spec, it sends the findings back as feedback, which Claude Code doesn't show as an error.
  - Only the stop and prompt hooks run the toolkit, as `spec` from the PATH. When it isn't installed, nothing is blocked, and the engineer sees a notice.
- **Alternatives:** Hooks that call the toolkit for everything, which costs a Python start-up with PyYAML on every tool call and fails on machines without the toolkit. A Claude Code plugin, which DR-1 ruled out.
- **Consequences:** A script that opens spec files itself, in python or awk, gets past the guard. The change log and the auditors are the backstop. The hook copy can fall behind the toolkit until `spec init` runs again.

### DR-41 🟡 ⤷SYS-14 Chat approvals are recorded only when they name items by ID, and anything else is confirmed first
*System elements:* AGENT · *Requirements:* AGENT-21, AGENT-33, AGENT-34, AGENT-43 · *Recorded:* round 11 (slice 3)
- **Context:** DR-6 has a hook record chat approvals: a message that starts with "approve" and names the items, or approves everything except some items. A hook can't tell which items "everything" covered in the agent's last message, or which items a described exception refers to (AGENT-43). It also can't see what the engineer was last shown (AGENT-34).
- **Decision:** The prompt hook reads each line of the engineer's message on its own. A line approves when it starts with "approve" (or "approved") and its first clause names only item IDs and ranges, or when it is only item IDs followed by "LGTM", "approved" or "looks good", as in "SYS-32 LGTM".
  - An ID may be written as a word and a number, such as "Change 13", when the word names a system element, needs or decision records (AGENT-57).
  - It records the whole message as the engineer's words, marked as given in chat, and tells the agent what it recorded.
  - Any other approval, such as "approve everything except the wording ones", records nothing. The hook tells the agent to show the exact list, leaving out every item an exception could refer to, and to get the engineer's confirmation, in a menu where the harness has one.
  - Quoted lines and pasted text never count, and a capitalized word counts as a system element only when that element exists. A message with "lgtm" or "looks good" and no IDs gets a note that it approves nothing.
- **Alternatives:** Reading "everything" as every unapproved item in the open change, which can approve items the engineer was never shown. Letting the agent interpret every approval, which DR-6 ruled out.
- **Consequences:** "Approve everything except …" costs one extra confirmation. An approval covers the items as they are when the engineer sends the message, and the hook asks the agent to say if it changed any of them after showing them. Claude Code also runs this hook for messages from other sessions and from background subagents, so an agent that sent a message starting with "approve" could create an approval. The skill forbids that, and each approval records its words.

### DR-42 🟡 ⤷SYS-11 The reasoning check's read guard refuses every read or search that could reach the spec
*System elements:* REASON · *Requirements:* REASON-5, REASON-2 · *Recorded:* round 11 (slice 3)
- **Context:** DR-7 planned a hook that refuses reads under the spec directory and drops spec hits from search results, and said to fall back to an instruction if that proved fiddly.
- **Decision:** The reasoning-check subagent gets only the read, search and file-listing tools. A hook refuses its reads inside the spec directory and its searches that could return a spec file.
  - A search reaches the spec when it starts inside it, or starts above it with no file filter or with a filter that matches a spec file.
  - Searches filtered to source files, or aimed at source directories, pass.
  - The hook is registered in the project's settings for every agent's reads, and acts only when the agent is the reasoning check. Claude Code skips hooks written in a subagent's own definition when the folder isn't trusted, which a live run showed.
- **Alternatives:** Filtering spec hits out of search results afterwards, which Claude Code allows but which means rewriting each tool's output format. The instruction alone.
- **Consequences:** The guard covers every tool the subagent has. A subagent that searches the whole repository without a filter is refused once, and narrows its search.

### DR-43 🟡 ⤷SYS-20 Rule links point at the rules page the repository has
*System elements:* CHECK · *Requirements:* CHECK-16 · *Recorded:* round 11 (slice 3)
- **Context:** The checker's findings link to the rule they break (CHECK-16). The rules page was docs/rules.md in the toolkit's repository, so links in every other repository pointed at a file that isn't there.
- **Decision:** The rules page is part of the skill. A finding links to the toolkit's own copy inside the toolkit's repository, else to the copy `spec init` installed, else to the page inside the installed package.
- **Alternatives:** A web address, which needs hosting and can disagree with the installed version.
- **Consequences:** In every repository the toolkit has set up, links are relative paths an editor can open.

### DR-44 🟡 🔓 Approval works like delegated authority in configuration management
*System elements:* SYS, MODEL, CHANGE, AGENT · *Requirements:* SYS-33, SYS-34, SYS-35, SYS-36, SYS-37, SYS-38, SYS-39, SYS-40 · *Recorded:* round 12 (spec-first)
- **Status:** built in round 12.
- **Context:** The engineer wants to approve the key points of the requirement tree, let agents decide the rest, and have each later change to what they approved, wrote or decided brought back to them (NEED-14 to NEED-20). Today every item needs approval, and over 200 items are waiting.
- **Decision:** Approval follows the split configuration management makes between a customer and a contractor (MIL-HDBK-61A, for example).
  - The engineer approves key items explicitly, as a customer approves a baseline. Everything beneath an approved item is delegated: the agent decides it, as a contractor decides the detailed design.
  - A change that alters an item the engineer approved, wrote or decided is like a Class I change: it goes back to the engineer once built and tested (SYS-37). Any other change is like a Class II change: the agent decides, and the change record logs it.
  - Whether an item is approved, delegated or neither is computed from the approvals and the tree each time it's shown, and never stored (SYS-40).
  - Where a requirement sits and whose words it carries are separate, as INCOSE keeps "trace to parent" apart from "trace to source": the system's structure places it (SYS-36), and it quotes the engineer's words it expresses (SYS-35).
- **Alternatives:** Approving every item, which is today's rule and doesn't scale. A stored importance score, which the engineer ruled out.
- **Consequences:** The engineer approves a few key items per change instead of every item. Agents need each item's approval state at the moment they change it (SYS-39). The merge check never blocks; it lists the alterations the engineer hasn't answered yet (CHECK-15, round 12 D1).

### DR-45 🟡 ⤷SYS-33 Approvals are kept as a history, each with who and how
*System elements:* MODEL, CLI · *Requirements:* MODEL-34, MODEL-35, CLI-11, CLI-12 · *Recorded:* round 12
- **Context:** The approvals file held one record per item, so approving again overwrote the earlier record and its words. SYS-33 asks what an approval says about who and how, and SYS-39 asks for history.
- **Decision:** Every approval is appended, never replaced, and each records the approver, the channel (terminal, chat, menu, page or restated), the date and time, how many items were approved together, the engineer's words, an optional note, and the resolved decisions that involved the item. An item's current approval is any record whose fingerprint matches its content, the latest one first.
- **Alternatives:** One record per item with a list of past approvals inside it, which makes the file harder to read in a diff. A separate history file, which splits what one approval means across two places.
- **Consequences:** The approvals file grows with every approval. Records from before round 12 lack the new fields, and the toolkit treats the missing fields as unknown.

### DR-46 🟡 ⤷SYS-35 The engineer's words go in a quotes list beside the older source field
*System elements:* MODEL, CHECK, REVIEW · *Requirements:* MODEL-36, CHECK-20, REVIEW-17 · *Recorded:* round 12
- **Context:** SYS-35 asks for the engineer's exact words with the date and time and the context. Existing items keep their words in a free-text `source` field, often with typos fixed and without dates.
- **Decision:** Items take a `quotes` list, each with `said`, `words` and `context`, and the checker requires all three. Existing `source` fields stay as they are. They aren't migrated, because their dates and contexts were never recorded and filling them in would mean inventing them.
- **Alternatives:** Migrating every `source` field with guessed dates, which would put invented metadata next to the engineer's words.
- **Consequences:** Two places hold the engineer's words until older items are revisited. The requirements view shows both, and its legend explains the difference.

### DR-47 🟡 🔒 An item's ancestors, for delegation, are what it traces to
*System elements:* CHECK · *Requirements:* CHECK-18, CHECK-19 · *Recorded:* round 12
- **Context:** Delegation needs a definition of "above" that covers every kind of item (DR-44).
- **Decision:** An item's ancestors are the needs a system requirement serves, the requirement an element requirement traces to, the requirements a verification item verifies, the requirements a decision record names, and a system element's parent, followed upward. An item is delegated under its nearest approved ancestor. An item that changed since its own approval isn't delegated: its change awaits the engineer. Nothing about the result is stored.
- **Alternatives:** Delegating only through the requirement tree, which would leave every verification item, decision record and element unreviewed.
- **Consequences:** Approving a need delegates everything beneath it, including system requirements. The agent's proposals (SYS-38) are how key items still reach the engineer.

### DR-48 🟡 ⤷CHANGE-13 Alterations to the engineer's items are flagged when logged, and answered by approval or rollback
*System elements:* CHANGE, CLI, CHECK · *Requirements:* CHANGE-13, CHANGE-14, CHECK-21 · *Recorded:* round 12
- **Context:** SYS-37 asks that each alteration to what the engineer approved, wrote or decided be raised after the work is built and tested, and the engineer described rolling back what they care about.
- **Decision:** When an edit changes the meaning of such an item, the change log records why it counts (approved, their words, their decision) and the item's fingerprints before and after. Before applying it, the CLI asks the agent to acknowledge it. The alteration stays listed in the change record, and as a to-do, until the engineer approves the item as it now is (kept), or it's back to its earlier content (rolled back). A removed item is listed but can't be kept by approval.
- **Alternatives:** Comparing against git history, which the toolkit doesn't read and which can't tell why an item counts. An explicit "answered" flag, which an agent could set without the engineer.
- **Consequences:** Alterations logged before round 12 carry no flag, so the mechanism starts with this round. Keeping an alteration is one line from the engineer, such as `CHECK-14 LGTM`.

### DR-49 🟡 ⤷SYS-30 Review sections carry their context inline instead of linking to it
*System elements:* REVIEW, CHANGE · *Requirements:* REVIEW-18, REVIEW-19 · *Recorded:* round 13
- **Context:** In round 12's record the engineer had to search for each proposed item's full text and scroll back. They read change records as raw Markdown in the editor, where links show no preview on hover.
- **Decision:** Wherever the change record asks the engineer to approve or answer for an item, it repeats what's needed to judge it right there: the full text, what it sits under, its rationale and the engineer's words; for a decision record, its reasoning and the full text of the requirements it decides. The other IDs the shown text mentions are listed with their titles.
- **Alternatives:** Linking each ID to its item with the text on hover, which only works in a Markdown preview. A glossary at the end of the record, which still means scrolling.
- **Consequences:** Change records get longer, and the same text can appear in two sections. Each review section can be read on its own.

### DR-50 🟡 ⤷SYS-7 Test links are checked by reading files, not by running tests
*System elements:* CHECK, LANG · *Requirements:* CHECK-4 · *Recorded:* round 14
- **Context:** Before a first real project, the engineer asked for a simple check that linked tests exist, with everything else scoped later.
- **Decision:** The checker confirms each link by reading the source: the file exists and, when the link names a test, the file declares it. That's a pytest function, with its class if given, or a GoogleTest declared with TEST, TEST_F, TEST_P or TYPED_TEST. Any other file only has to mention the name. Links resolve against the implementation's root, and `spec edit` checks them against the real repository rather than its scratch copy.
- **Alternatives:** Asking pytest and the test binary to list their tests, which needs a built project and is slow. Checking only that the file exists, which misses the commonest error: a renamed or misspelled test.
- **Consequences:** Listing tests no verification item links to (CHECK-3), the rest of the language adapters (LANG-3) and running tests stay unbuilt until a real project shows what they need. A test generated by a macro other than these isn't recognized.

### DR-51 🟡 ⤷SYS-5 Setup points sessions at the skill and lets agents run everyday commands
*System elements:* CLI, AGENT · *Requirements:* CLI-16, CLI-20 · *Recorded:* round 14
- **Context:** The engineer put the agent in charge of agent experience. In a live run, every toolkit command waited for permission, and nothing told a new session the method existed.
- **Decision:** `spec init` writes a short section between markers into AGENTS.md, or CLAUDE.md when that's the file the repository has, and rewrites only that section on later runs. It adds Claude Code allow rules for status, check, show, render, edit, change, decide, propose and friction. Approve and resolve stay with the permission prompt, so the engineer confirms each command that records their words.
- **Alternatives:** Relying on the skill's description to trigger, which a quick request may not do. Allowing every toolkit command, which would let an approval be recorded without the engineer seeing it.
- **Consequences:** Claude Code ignores a project's allow rules until the engineer has trusted the folder once, interactively. `--no-instructions` leaves the instruction files alone.

### DR-52 🟡 ⤷SYS-5 Agents and hooks run the toolkit as `spec` from the PATH
*System elements:* CLI, AGENT · *Requirements:* SYS-5, SYS-32, CLI-9, CLI-15 · *Recorded:* round 15
- **Context:** The engineer asked why agents had to type `.syseng/spec` instead of installing the toolkit so that `spec` is simply on the PATH. The launchers (DR-39) existed so agents and hooks could find a toolkit installed in a virtual environment their shell hadn't activated, and to fit the engineer's Nix setup, which the engineer had asked not to design around.
- **Decision:** The toolkit is installed with a Python tool installer, `pipx install` or `uv tool install`, which puts `spec` on the PATH in an isolated environment. `--editable` runs a checkout, so changes to the toolkit apply at once. Agents, messages, the skill and the hooks all use plain `spec`.
  - `spec init` no longer writes launchers, removes the one earlier setups wrote, and says when `spec` isn't on the PATH.
  - `.syseng/hook` stays in the repository, using only the standard library, so the guards keep working on a clone whose machine lacks the toolkit.
- **Alternatives:** The two launchers (DR-39), which solved the same problem the standard tools solve, at the cost of a longer command, a file outside the repository and extra code. Installing into a project's virtual environment, which agents' shells often don't activate.
- **Consequences:** Each machine needs the toolkit on its PATH, and the setup notice says how. One toolkit version serves every repository on a machine. A different program named `spec` earlier on the PATH would shadow the toolkit.

### DR-53 🟡 ⤷SYS-5 The skill and subagents are installed once per machine, as links to the installed toolkit
*System elements:* CLI, AGENT · *Requirements:* CLI-9, CLI-21, AGENT-42 · *Recorded:* round 17
- **Context:** With a copy of the skill in every repository, an update to the toolkit reached a repository only when someone ran setup there and committed the result, and a repository's copy could disagree with the `spec` installed on the machine. The engineer asked how updates would reach their other repositories, and chose the user-level location.
- **Decision:** `spec init` links the user-level folders to the installed toolkit: ~/.claude/skills/syseng and the two subagents in ~/.claude/agents for Claude Code, and ~/.hermes/skills/syseng for Hermes when Hermes is set up on the machine.
  - With an editable install, an edit to the toolkit reaches every repository at once. Otherwise, upgrading the toolkit does.
  - A repository keeps its spec, the instruction-file section, and Claude Code's hook script and settings. Setup removes the copies earlier setups put in repositories.
  - A skill or subagent of the engineer's own at those paths is left alone.
  - Antigravity, with no user-level folder known, still gets a copy in the repository.
- **Alternatives:** A copy per repository, refreshed by setup and flagged when stale, which keeps each repository self-contained at the cost of a commit per update per repository. A Claude Code plugin, which DR-1 ruled out.
- **Consequences:** The skill an agent follows always matches the `spec` command it describes. A machine needs the toolkit installed and setup run once before its sessions get the skill. Claude Code's cloud sessions don't read user-level skills.
